title: Latent usage chords and actionable asks - customer synth
content:
TL;DR:
This is a compact synthesis of recurring customer signals we observed across Q4 usage logs, support threads, and syncs. I grouped behavior into three "usage chords" (slow-concurrent bursts, long-prefix chat sessions, and low-QPS high-token analytics) and mapped them to 9 actionable asks. Prioritization is biased toward low-risk, high-customer-impact patches that reduce token cost or improve steady latency for hosted users.

What I looked at (sources):
- Support threads: 24 threads tagged "latency" or "cost" (Nov–Dec 2025)
- Instrumented request logs (anonymized): sampled 5k sessions across 12 accounts flagged by CSMs
- Customer calls: notes from 6 post-implementation reviews (CS/solutions eng)
- A/B rollout telemetry: 3 early rollouts where model fallback was used

High-level signal (one-liner):
Many customers are not just sensitive to average per-token cost — they experience pain at specific usage rhythms (the chords). Small platform-level patches (KV cache visibility, per-route token accounting, prompt-length alerts, graceful model fallbacks) would defuse many asks.

Usage chords (novel framing to help engineering prioritize patterns):
1) Slow-concurrent bursts ("heartbeat" pattern)
   - Description: Hundreds of concurrent short chats (1–3 turns), interleaved with frequent reconnects from mobile clients. Each chat has small token lengths but high concurrency causes queueing and tail latency spikes on shared hosts.
   - Customer quote (edited): "Our app opens thousands of tiny sessions per minute — p95 latency jumps to 800ms and users feel lag even though avg latency is fine."

2) Long-prefix chat sessions ("long-lived context")
   - Description: Single chat with very long pinned context (context windows > 8k tokens). Customers pin a long knowledge base and then run many shorter completions against it. This amplifies KV cache pressure and increases memory churn on hosts.
   - Customer ask: better cache affordances + telemetry to know when prefix reuse is happening.

3) Low-QPS, high-token analytics ("batch analytics")
   - Description: Periodic offline jobs that send very large prompts for reranking / summarization. These jobs are cost-sensitive and want quantization recommendations and near-deterministic throughput.
   - Customer quote: "We run nightly summarization of 10k docs — we just need predictable throughput, not streaming interactivity."

Top 9 actionable asks (rough priority, estimated effort, suggested owner):
A. Surface per-route token/latency breakdown in Console and API (low effort; owner: console-and-rollouts)
   - Why: Customers repeatedly ask for token-level charge visibility to map product flows to dollars.
   - Proposed minimal: show p50/p95 token counts and cost estimates per API key + per-route.
   - Quick win: wire in existing tokenization lib and add a lightweight UI panel.

B. KV-cache reuse telemetry + heuristic hints (medium effort; owner: serving-runtime)
   - Why: Long-prefix sessions cause cache thrash. Customers want to know when the cache is reused and when it’s not.
   - Proposed: a per-request header/metric: KV_HIT=true/false + reuse_ratio estimate.
   - Risk: may add tracing overhead; keep sampling rate low. See JIRA-4521 for prototype perf numbers.

C. Per-route graceful fallback policies (medium effort; owner: platform-engineering)
   - Why: Several customers requested deterministic fallback behaviors when a dedicated pool is warm but momentarily saturated.
   - Proposed: allow per-route policy: immediate-fallback | retry-then-fallback | queue-with-max-wait.

D. Prompt-length alerts and best-practice checklist for clients (low effort; owner: developer-experience)
   - Why: Many customers send accidental huge prefixes (copy-paste KBs). An alert could avoid unnecessary cost.
   - Proposed: server-side heuristic + Console notification + opt-in auto-truncate suggestion.

E. Dedicated small-burst capacity lanes (medium effort; owner: dedicated)
   - Why: The heartbeat pattern needs predictable tail latency; customers prefer a smaller reserved pool tuned for high concurrency of short requests.
   - Proposed: a SKU that guarantees max-p95 latency for N concurrent short requests. Align with billing.

F. Batch-mode submission API for large analytics jobs (low–mid effort; owner: hosted-api)
   - Why: Batch jobs currently contend with interactive traffic. Separate lane + different cost accounting makes sense.
   - Proposed: POST /batch-jobs with estimated tokens, non-streaming, prioritized scheduling window.

G. Model-pin per-tenant + visibility for rollouts (medium effort; owner: private-deployments/product-hosted-api)
   - Why: Enterprise customers need deterministic behavior during canaries and A/B.
   - Proposed: console toggle + API flag to pin to a model family/version; show active pin in per-tenant view.

H. Cost-optimized quantization recommendations (research/medium effort; owner: applied-ml/optimize)
   - Why: Customers running reranking/analytics want recommended model variant/quantization with cost/quality tradeoff.
   - Proposed: a 1–2 page report generated after a dry-run (example: 4-bit int8 suggestion + expected throughput uplift).

I. Lightweight prompt caching at SDK level (low effort; owner: developer-experience)
   - Why: Many apps repeat identical few-turn prompts across users. An SDK opt-in cache reduces repeat token costs.
   - Proposed: an LRU cache with TTL that can be toggled per-route.

Customer vignettes (short):
- Fintech startup (mid-market): heartbeat pattern — uses Redwood for question/answering on transactions. They saw 10–15% cost bump from repeated prefix resends. Want per-route token breakdown + SDK cache.
- Healthcare enterprise (private deployment): long-prefix sessions — pinned patient context, needs KV reuse telemetry + deterministic fallbacks. Concerned about audit logs for model pinning.
- ML platform (analytics): nightly reranks — prefers batch API and quantization guidance to cut e2e run time.

Open questions / constraints:
- Telemetry cost: how much extra cardinality can we safely add before metrics cost spikes? (ask observability team)
- UX: how do we present per-route dollars in a way that won’t confuse non-technical PMs? (design session needed)
- Billing implications for SKU suggestions (dedicated small-burst lane): need pricing ops input.

Possible quick experiments (<=2 week effort each):
1) Add console panel for per-route recent token histogram (sampled) + sample UI mock; measure usage.
2) Server-side sampled header KV_HIT flag emitted for 1% of requests from 3 pilot customers.
3) SDK opt-in LRU cache release to 5 internal apps and 2 customers (toy telemetry).

Risk notes (engineering):
- Sampling rate decisions: if too low we miss patterns; too high we increase cost. Start small and iterate.
- Backwards compatibility: adding headers/flags should be opt-in initially for private and dedicated.
- Billing/contract risk: introducing dedicated small-burst SKUs may need updates to enterprise contracts. Coordinate with sales.

Next steps (owner + due dates):
- Aisha: draft product brief for per-route token panel (delivery: 2026-01-22)
- Tomás: prototype server header for KV_HIT sampling (delivery: 2026-01-29) — link to JIRA-4521
- Maya: design quick mockups for console panel and billing tooltip (delivery: 2026-01-21)
- Evan: talk to pricing ops about small-burst SKU feasibility (meeting 2026-01-19)

Notes to self / follow-ups:
- Pull the 5k-session anonymized sample into Data Studio to visualize chord clusters (use tag "heartbeat").
- Ask SRE for memory footprint breakouts on long-prefix sessions (tracked in GH issue 598).

Appendix: raw snippets from customer threads (anonymized)
- "We would pay for a smaller pool that serves small requests quickly — right now we pay for throughput but the tails still hurt us."
- "If there was an easy way to see which routes rack up tokens, we could redesign the flows."
- "We accidentally pushed a KB dump in production and blew our token budget overnight — an opt-in prompt truncation or warning would have saved us."

End of doc.

-- Aisha (notes are intentionally compact; will expand into product brief once we sync with eng/design)
